title: EU anti-dumping duties imposed on cold-rolled flat steel from India, Japan, Taiwan, Turkiye, Vietnam
intro: Trade defence dominates today's edition. The European Union has imposed anti-dumping duties on cold-rolled flat steel from India, Japan, Taiwan, Turkiye and Vietnam, according to Goodreturns. Shanghai Metals Market reports that the duties have started with no retroactive collection. Brussels is also proposing to extend its carbon border mechanism to 180 downstream steel and aluminium products. In China, BigMint reports iron ore prices at a near four-year low as weak steel prices curb mill buying. In the United States, Nippon Steel is reviving a Pennsylvania mill with an investment of nearly 3 billion USD. Most of today's material consists of headlines without publisher excerpts, so detail is limited and we say so where it matters.

analysis: Analysis: Today's reports suggest that European steel policy is tightening on two fronts at once. The cold-rolled anti-dumping duties, together with HRC reportedly holding at highs, could support European mill margins in the near term. However, they may raise costs for downstream buyers. If the Commission's proposal to extend CBAM to 180 downstream products proceeds, it could address the concern that carbon costs simply shift to imported finished goods. Indian exporters of cold-rolled flat steel will need to reassess European volumes, although the material does not give company-specific margins. Salzgitter's call for affordable power and Voestalpine's trimmed outlook point to a recurring tension: decarbonisation projects advance while operating economics remain under strain. Elsewhere, a near four-year low in Chinese iron ore prices, driven by weak steel prices, could indicate continued softness in Chinese demand. That could keep export pressure on global markets, which helps explain the spread of trade defences. In the United States, Nippon Steel's Pennsylvania investment and Nucor's record shipments suggest domestic capacity is being reinforced. Readers should note that these inferences rest on headlines rather than full reports.
